glyph_groups.exception_failed_on: criterion 1 (no visible context distinguishes the inert pills before the tap) and criterion 4 (nothing a first-time user could read tells them the selected chip decides whether SET works)
glyph_groups.evidence: all 20 "SET" pills tapped on their live states. The 13 pills shown while the PDF chip is selected (screen1, 2, 3, 10, 15, 16, 18, 19, 26, 31, 32, 34, 35) each opened the "Set as default" bottom sheet. The 7 pills shown while HWP, Word, Excel or PPT is selected (screen6, 7, 8, 9, 22, 23, 25) did nothing at all — no sheet, no navigation, no change; re-tested by hand on HWP (twice, including a tap on the pill's own record), Word, Excel and PPT with 5-second waits, with a PDF-chip control tap in between that did open the sheet. Same picture, same banner text beside it ("Set as default reader"), two behaviours. Context exception considered and declined: criterion 1 fails — the only thing on screen that differs is which file-type chip is selected above and the pill's colour, and neither says that SET will be inert; criterion 4 fails — a first-time user reads "Set as default reader  SET" identically on every chip and cannot know the chip decides whether it works.
glyph_groups.recommendation: make SET open the set-as-default sheet on every chip, or hide the banner on the chips where it cannot act; never show an inert SET beside the words "Set as default reader"

Formed by testing (grouping correction): the left chevron had no function string, and the "Settings" title was declared only by its own word. Tapping showed both do the same job — each leaves Settings and returns to the screen it was opened from (title tapped on the word and again at x=700, far from the chevron, on both screens). Confusion bullets that apply: (1) both renderings sit on the same toolbar doing the same job at the same scope, with nothing to say they are the same thing; (2) they co-occur side by side and read as two different things — one a back control, the other a heading; (3) the title's rendering collides with a different job: the word "Settings" names the place the user is in, and elsewhere in the app reaching Settings is what the gear does, so a heading that says "Settings" and throws the user out of Settings borrows a label that means the opposite. No surface, scope or explicitness argument rescues it — the title is less explicit about "back" than the chevron, not more.
function_groups.confusion_falls_on: a user who taps the heading "Settings" (to read it, to scroll, or expecting the options it names) and is thrown out of Settings, losing their place with nothing on screen having warned them
function_groups.recommendation: make the title non-interactive and leave "back" to the chevron alone; if the whole toolbar must stay tappable, make it do nothing rather than navigate

function_groups.evidence: From a candidate (evidence: near_miss_key). All 22 "Allow Access" buttons and both "GO TO SET" buttons tapped: every one left the app for the same Android "All files access" page. Confusion bullets that apply: (1) the two renderings co-occur — on screen14/30 the "GO TO SET" dialog is drawn over the Home tab with "Allow Access" still visible behind it — and read as two different options for one job; (2) "GO TO SET" is the less explicit rendering: it names neither access nor files, and a user who learned "Allow Access" has nothing linking the two; (3) it collides with a different job's appearance: the word "SET" is exactly the banner pill (gg14) visible on the same screen, which opens the set-as-default sheet, so "GO TO SET" reads as a continuation of that job rather than of "Allow Access". No surface or scope argument holds: both are full-width dark pill buttons asking for the same permission.
function_groups.confusion_falls_on: a user who learned "Allow Access" on the Home tab and then meets "GO TO SET" in the dialog (reached from the scan button or any Tools tile), and anyone who connects "SET" with the default-reader banner beside it
function_groups.recommendation: label the dialog button with the same words as the Home button ("Allow Access"), or with the destination in full ("Open settings to allow file access"); avoid the bare word "SET" for two different jobs
